title: Heredity
standard_code: JSS 3 Intermediate Science: Living and Non-Living Things
standard_text: Traits are passed from parents to offspring through genes on chromosomes; dominant and recessive alleles; Punnett squares predict the results of monohybrid crosses; incomplete dominance, codominance and sex-linked traits. (summary of the Intermediate Science curriculum, JSS 3, theme: Living and Non-Living Things)
meta_desc: Free JSS 3 Intermediate Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Living and Non-Living Things): genes and alleles, dominant and recessive traits, Punnett squares, incomplete and codominance and sex-linked traits. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Offspring get one allele from each parent.
body_html:
How to think about it

Genes on chromosomes carry the instructions for traits. Each person has two alleles for each gene, one from each parent. A dominant allele (T) shows when present; a recessive allele (t) shows only when there are two copies (tt).

A Punnett square predicts the offspring of a cross: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 3 tall : 1 short. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is in between (red × white gives pink); in codominance both show (blood type AB). Some traits are carried on the X chromosome.

Example

Tt × tt. Fraction with the recessive trait?

Punnett square

Answer: 1/2

Example

Genotype of a person with blood type O?

Recessive

Answer: ii

Common mistakes

  • Thinking dominant means more common.
  • Mixing up genotype and phenotype.
  • Forgetting that each parent gives only one allele.

faq.q: Why can two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child?
faq.a: Both can carry a recessive allele and pass it on.

faq.q: Why is colour blindness more common in males?
faq.a: The allele is on the X chromosome, and males have only one X.

items.q: What causes Turner's syndrome?
c: an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY)
lack of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine
a missing X chromosome in a female (XO)
items.e: Turner's syndrome: a missing X chromosome in a female (XO).

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is not a carrier and the father is colour-blind. What is the chance a son is colour-blind?
items.e: Sons get their X from their mother; daughters get one X from each parent.

items.q: Which mechanism of sex determination is found in humans and Drosophila?
items.e: Humans and Drosophila: XX–XY (male heterogametic).

items.q: Which mechanism of sex determination is found in honey bees?
items.e: Honey bees: haplodiploidy (males develop from unfertilised eggs).

items.q: What causes Klinefelter's syndrome?
c: an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY)
a missing X chromosome in a female (XO)
a protein needed for blood clotting is missing
items.e: Klinefelter's syndrome: an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY).

items.q: Which disorder is caused by lack of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine?
items.e: Phenylketonuria: lack of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine.

items.q: What causes haemophilia?
c: a protein needed for blood clotting is missing
a missing X chromosome in a female (XO)
an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY)
items.e: Haemophilia: a protein needed for blood clotting is missing.

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is a carrier and the father is not colour-blind. What is the chance a daughter is colour-blind?

items.q: What is the law of segregation?
c: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation
items.e: Each gamete gets one allele.
